messages.body_plain:
Special Issue on Data Analysis for Behavioral Medicine

A special issue of the Journal of Behavioral Medicine seeks original research papers and tutorials that advance quantitative methods utilized in behavioral medicine and health psychology research.

Special Issue Guest Editors

Mauricio Garnier-Villarreal, PhD

Alexander Schoemann, PhD

Manshu Yang, PhD

Important Dates

Abstract Deadline: 9/15/2024

Manuscript Submission Deadline: 12/16/2024

Background

Methods and theory are intertwined in behavioral research; theoretical developments lead to the need for new methods to test theories, and the development of new methods can advance theories. To continue to advance research in behavior medicine, new methods need to be developed and implemented. At the same time, data collected in studies of behavioral medicine are increasing in complexity and advanced quantitative methods, which are accessible to researchers, are required to analyze these data.

Special Issue Objectives

In this special issue, we welcome contributions to the development and dissemination of methods for collecting, analyzing, and interpreting data as well as teaching applied researchers how to implement quantitative methods that are increasingly used in health-related research. To help the dissemination of quantitative methods among behavioral medicine researchers, authors are encouraged to maintain a substantive focus over a technical one.

Example areas of research include, but are not limited to:

●       Latent variable models

●       Bayesian statistics

●       Longitudinal data analysis methods

●       Multilevel modeling

●       Causal inference

●       Missing data analysis

We are also interested in tutorial papers focused on the application of advanced methods, or methods not commonly used in behavioral medicine.

.

Manuscript Submission

An abstract of no more than 400 words should be submitted to Alexander Schoemann (schoe...@ecu.edu) by September 15, 2024. The editors will provide feedback to the authors on the abstract and only a subset of proposals will be invited to submit a full manuscript. All submitted manuscripts will undergo peer review. Approval to submit a manuscript does not guarantee inclusion in the special issue. Manuscripts should follow the instructions for regular articles or brief reports, respectively, and be submitted via the online submission system on the journal’s website (https://www.springer.com/journal/10865). The cover letter should specify that the authors wish their manuscript to be considered for the Special Issue on Data Analysis for  Behavioral Medicine.

messages.body_plain:
Hi all,

I am fitting 3 different models (that frequently occur in the literature) to a dataset of n=98. Missingness has been handled through mice and I am running the cfa.mi() function to fit all my models.

Each model is fitted through this line of code:

fit<- cfa.mi(fit, data = list_imp_data, estimator = "MLR")

The three different models are a 6, 5 and 1 factor model and both the 6-factor and 1-factor model are fitted without any warnings messages. However, when fitting the five factor model I receive the following warning message:

Warning message:
lavaan->lav_object_post_check():
   covariance matrix of latent variables is not positive definite ; use lavInspect(fit, "cov.lv <http://cov.lv>") to investigate.

The model is not under-identified as the warning message would have me believe but I am assuming this warning message is returned even under other conditions than whether the model is identified or not. I have inspected the correlation matrix and have not found any extreme coefficients in the observed data. However, looking at the latent variables (LV) covariances I can see a pair with a covariance of 0.94. Could this be the cause of the problem? When inspecting the covariance of the LV in the 6-factor model some LV covary with 0.9 but the majority sit at around 0.5-0.6.

What could explain the warning message I receive?

Best regards
Adam

Did you specify any of the indicators as ordinal when doing CFA? If you did, and the numbers of unique values in one or more ordinal indicators are not the same, then the number of parameters can be different, as shown below:

``` r
library(lavaan)
#> This is lavaan 0.6-18
#> lavaan is FREE software! Please report any bugs.
```

``` r

dat <- HolzingerSwineford1939

# Artificially convert the scores to 2 or 3 values
dat$x1 <- ifelse(dat$school == "Grant-White", cut(dat$x1, breaks = 3), cut(dat$x1, breaks = 2))
dat$x2 <- ifelse(dat$school == "Grant-White", cut(dat$x2, breaks = 3), cut(dat$x2, breaks = 2))
dat$x3 <- ifelse(dat$school == "Grant-White", cut(dat$x3, breaks = 3), cut(dat$x3, breaks = 2))
dat$x4 <- ifelse(dat$school == "Grant-White", cut(dat$x4, breaks = 3), cut(dat$x4, breaks = 2))

# Verify that the numbers of categorieas are different
xtabs(~ x1 + school, dat)
#>    school
#> x1  Grant-White Pasteur
#>   1          15      56
#>   2         100     100
#>   3          30       0
```

``` r
xtabs(~ x2 + school, dat)
#>    school
#> x2  Grant-White Pasteur
#>   1           4      85
#>   2         105      71

```


> > does that mean that is not possible with lavaan to get same indices of modification as Mplus?
>
> That means lavaan will not provide them for you.  But I think it should be pretty easy to apply the scale/shift correction to each modification index yourself.
>
> chisq.scaled = (chisq × scaling.factor) + shift.parameter
>
> The summary() output shows the scale/shift parameters below the robust test.
>
> example(lavTables)
> fit
>
> You can access those values more directly (as R objects) using the lavTest() function
>
> (TEST <- lavTest(fit, test = "scaled.shifted"))
>
> Then apply those values to the $mi column of modindices() output.
>
> MI <- modindices(fit)
> MI$mi.scaled <- MI$mi * TEST$scaling.factor + TEST$shift.parameter
> MI
>
> Notice that the rank-order of indices is identical before/after transformation.
>
> cor(MI$mi, MI$mi.scaled, method = "spearman")
>
> So the same "most important indices" would be flagged.  But using the common arbitrary "only indices > 10" criterion, only the scaled/shifted ones have 2 flagged parameters (which is consistent with the naive test not being significant, p = .156, whereas the scaled/shifted test has p = .031)
>
>
> Terrence D. Jorgensen    (he, him, his)

messages.subject: Missing = "ML" vs missing = "FIML"
messages.body_plain:
Dear all,

I hope you are well.

I just have a simple questions about how to request Full Information ML for missing data in Lavaan. The tutorial says that to use Full Information ML, missing = "ML" is required in the function. Particularly, it says that:

If the data contain missing values, the default behavior is listwise deletion. If the missing mechanism is MCAR (missing completely at random) or MAR (missing at random), the lavaan package provides case-wise (or ‘full information’) maximum likelihood estimation. You can turn this feature on, by using the argument missing = "ML" when calling the fitting function. An unrestricted (h1) model will automatically be estimated, so that all common fit indices are available.

However, I've seen people here (and elsewhere) suggesting that FIML is actually requested when doing missing = "FIML". For example, in this question in Research Gate, Holger says that to request FIML estimator, one needs to use missing = "FIML" (https://www.researchgate.net/post/How-to-resolve-an-issue-in-R-with-lavaan-installed-using-the-FIML-function).

Can someone help clarify this issue? Specifically, is FIML requested with missing = "FIML" or "ML" or both? And if there is any difference, what is the difference?

Kind regards,
Maximiliano

messages.body_plain:
> Does lavaan automatically select the appropriate estimator for ordered data? If not, which estimator would you recommend using?

When you declare any endogenous variables as ordered=, the default is DWLS estimation.  The SEs and model-fit test will be corrected to account for the two-stage estimation (first thresholds+polychorics, then fit the SEM to those).

> Can I only test for configural invariance, weak invariance (loadings), and strong invariance (loadings and thresholds) with ordered data?

Search the forum for posts about measurement invariance with categorical indicators.  Your order is wrong, perpetuated by decades of bad advice.  Read the Wu & Estabrook (2016) reference on the ?semTools::measEq.syntax help page, and follow the examples.

> Which fit indices should be reported (scalar, robust)?

The ones labeled "robust" are consistent estimates of the index that would be obtained from normal data.

> Is there a built-in method for comparing two or more models, for example, using semTools?

Use lavaan::lavTestLRT()

> Which fit indices would you recommend reporting (e.g., CFI, TLI, RMSEA, and SRMR)?

No single-number summary is really useful to describe why a model fails to reproduce the data.

> When comparing the Comparative Fit Index (CFI), for two models should I compare the robust or the scalar CFI?

That is not a valid way to test equivalence of 2 nested models.

> Are there any tutorials or guidelines online that you would recommend? I would be happy to cite any relevant tutorial if available.

This is available: https://doi.org/10.1080/10705511.2019.1602776

> I had some missing pattern in one item and I decided to remove it, but I was wondering if there is any way to also include this item (error: lavaan->lav_samplestats_step1():      some categories of variable `AmasS07' are empty in group 1)

 You can collapse 2 adjacent categories to avoid that.  It is possible to fit models with different parameters per group, but that takes a lot more effort to manually specify all your syntax.

     I am getting ready to deliver a session at the American Psychological Association conference next month where I will be demonstrating a variety of composite-based approaches for SEM. One general approach involves factor scores. But my calculations are not producing the results that I expect.
     I have a model where the correlation matrix of the standardized common factors is:
1.00

1.00 - a
0.50       1.00 - b
0.25       0.50       1.00 - c
where a, b and c are positive quantities reflecting the indeterminacy of the factor scores for each factor. The difference between correct factor scores and regression method factor scores is that correct scores include an orthogonal random variable--call it z1, z2, z3--for each common factor, weighted based on the indeterminacy associated with each factor.

0.853
0.476   0.754
0.247   0.474  0.837

messages.body_plain:
Hello Ed,

First of all, the 0.99998 values on the diagonal are due to the fact
that you used cov() when applying the Bollen-Stine adjustment, and this
is using N-1 (instead of N). Since lavaan is using ML estimation per
default, we insist on using N. You can fix this as follows:

bigout.sat <- sem(model=model.sat,data=bigovdat,auto.fix.first=F,
std.lv <http://std.lv>=T, sample.cov.rescale = FALSE)

and you will get 1.0 again. But that is just a small detail, and has
nothing to do with your problem.

On 7/6/24 5:43 PM, Edward Rigdon wrote:
>       But I'm not getting that. For the regression method factor scores,
> I'm getting:
> 0.853
> 0.476   0.754
> 0.247   0.474  0.837
> So the covariances are not what I expect. And I can't quite figure out why.

I am afraid you had the wrong expectation. For 'regression' factor
scores, both the variances AND covariances will be off (compared to the
covariance matrix of the latent variables).

To get them right, you need to apply the following 'corrections' (often
used Croon's corrections). Starting from the saturated CFA model:

bigout.sat<-sem(model=model.sat,data=bigovdat,auto.fix.first=F,
std.lv <http://std.lv>=T, sample.cov.rescale = FALSE)

rmsat <- lavPredict(bigout.sat)
VETA_reg <- cov(rmsat)

ests<-lavInspect(bigout.sat,what = "estimates")
lambda <-ests$lambda
psi <-ests$psi
theta <- ests$theta
sigma.alt<-lavTech(bigout.sat,"fitted")
sigma.alt<-matrix(sigma.alt[[1]][[1]],nrow=9,byrow=T)
mult <-psi %*% t(lambda) %*% solve(sigma.alt)

and now we can compute

D <- mult %*% lambda
D.inv <- solve(D)
E <- mult %*% theta %*% t(mult)

and apply the corrections:

D.inv %*% (VETA_reg - E) %*% t(D.inv)

      f1  f2   f3
f1 1.00 0.5 0.25
f2 0.50 1.0 0.50
f3 0.25 0.5 1.00

Perhaps you were thinking about Bartlett factor scores? Then, the
covariances will be spot on, (but the variances will be still off):

tmp <- lavPredict(bigout.std, method = "Bartlett")
round(cov(tmp), 3)

      f1    f2    f3
f1 1.18 0.500 0.250
f2 0.50 1.395 0.500
f3 0.25 0.500 1.203

To fix the variances, we need the Bartlett factor score matrix:

A <- solve(t(lambda) %*% solve(theta) %*% lambda) %*% t(lambda) %*%
solve(theta)

and the correction for the variances are on the diagonal of

E <- A %*% theta %*% t(A)

Applying the correction:

VETA_bartlett <- cov(tmp)
round(VETA_bartlett - E, 3)

      f1  f2   f3
f1 1.00 0.5 0.25
f2 0.50 1.0 0.50
f3 0.25 0.5 1.00

See Appendix D in

Rosseel, Y., & Loh, W. W. (2022). A Structural After Measurement
Approach to Structural Equation Modeling. Psychological Methods. Advance
online publication. https://dx.doi.org/10.1037/met0000503

Yves.

I'd be a bit worried about my model. It looks like you're right on the edge of acceptability. A non-admissible solution means that Lavaan found an answer but the answer that it found can't exist in the real world (e.g. a negative variance).  This is normally a sign that your model is misspecified. If bootstrap resamples have a problem, it means that you are very close to an unacceptable model. Maybe you can say "Well, more than 3/4 of the models were acceptable, so I'll go for it", maybe you can add a constraint, for example, in a growth model, you sometimes need to fix the variance of a slope to zero, which means that there is no variance in the slope - this could be OK, everyone has the same slope.  Maybe, as Terrence says about, use Satorra-Bentler - why do you need to bootstrap?

Jeremy

messages.subject: Re: measurement invariance for ordinal variables
messages.body_plain:
> Could you point me towards work that would support my strategy to test the following MI sequence: factor patterns (configural), loadings (metric), thresholds (threshold), intercepts (scalar) and unique variances (residual MI)?

No, thresholds must be equated before any parameters that depend on the latent-response scale.

> Or rather, how come that you also disagree with the notion that thresholds are the intercept-equivalent in ordered data?

https://doi.org/10.1007/s11336-016-9506-0

> This is especially important to my case, since I only have three response categories and therefore the configural and threshold model have the same degrees of freedom - ergo they have the same fit in this case.

Correct, with 3 categories, you only have 2 thresholds per item, which you can trade for 2 latent-response parameters (intercept and residual/marginal variance).  So you can't test threshold invariance, only assume it.  Therefore, the first test you conduct is to compare any configural model to one that constraints both loadings and thresholds (without constraining intercepts or variances).

Terrence D. Jorgensen
Assistant Professor, Methods and Statistics
Research Institute for Child Development and Education, the University of Amsterdam

Hi folks,

I am trying to simulate a sem dataset and fit it with a CFA model:

m <- "f1 =~ 0.7*A1 + 0.7*A2 + 0.7*A3 + 0.7*A4 + 0.7*A5
      A2 ~ 0.2*A1"

         A2 ~ A1

fit <- lavaan::cfa(model = mcfa, data = d,
                   std.lv <http://std.lv> = TRUE)

I expected the residual variances of A2 would be ~0.47 since it equals latent variances minus factor loading square minus regression coefficient square (i.e., 1 - 0.7^2 - 0.2^2 = 0.47). But the model summary gave me different results:

summary(fit)

Latent Variables:
                   Estimate  Std.Err  z-value  P(>|z|)
  f1 =~
    A1                0.702    0.001  710.381    0.000
    A2                0.702    0.001  538.919    0.000
    A3                0.700    0.001  741.781    0.000
    A4                0.702    0.001  743.488    0.000

   .A5                0.511    0.001  575.473    0.000

Since the regression coefficient was recovered, I assumed the model was correctly specified..? But I am confused about A2's residuals; why was that 0.274 rather than 0.47? Any idea how lavaan::cfa() calculates the residual of A2? Any help will be highly appreciated :)

messages.body_plain:
Working on some functionality to wrap efa scripting in lavaan, and noticed some df's that seemed off, and wondering if I'm goofing/overlooking something, or rather, if something unexpected or errant is going on by using cfa() to fit these models (as done, at one point, in the EFA lavaan tutorial/example <https://lavaan.ugent.be/tutorial/efa.html>)

To use the same example (and if comfortable), installing the package I develop (which has the built-in data set im using):

install.packages("dySEM")

library(dySEM)
library(lavaan)

dat <- commitmentQ

fac1.script <- "
#Measurement Model

#Loadings
efa('efa')*f1 =~ sat.g.1_1+sat.g.1_2+sat.g.1_3+sat.g.1_4+sat.g.1_5 + sat.g.2_1+sat.g.2_2+sat.g.2_3+sat.g.2_4+sat.g.2_5

#Residual Variances
sat.g.1_1 ~~ sat.g.1_1
sat.g.1_2 ~~ sat.g.1_2
sat.g.1_3 ~~ sat.g.1_3
sat.g.1_4 ~~ sat.g.1_4
sat.g.1_5 ~~ sat.g.1_5

sat.g.2_1 ~~ sat.g.2_1
sat.g.2_2 ~~ sat.g.2_2
sat.g.2_3 ~~ sat.g.2_3
sat.g.2_4 ~~ sat.g.2_4
sat.g.2_5 ~~ sat.g.2_5

#Residual Covariances
sat.g.1_1 ~~ sat.g.2_1
sat.g.1_2 ~~ sat.g.2_2
sat.g.1_3 ~~ sat.g.2_3
sat.g.1_4 ~~ sat.g.2_4
sat.g.1_5 ~~ sat.g.2_5
"

fac2.script <- "
#Measurement Model

#Loadings
efa("efa")*f1 +
efa("efa")*f2 =~ sat.g.1_1 + sat.g.1_2 + sat.g.1_3 + sat.g.1_4 + sat.g.1_5 + sat.g.2_1 + sat.g.2_2 + sat.g.2_3 + sat.g.2_4 + sat.g.2_5

#Residual Variances
sat.g.1_1 ~~ sat.g.1_1
sat.g.1_2 ~~ sat.g.1_2
sat.g.1_3 ~~ sat.g.1_3
sat.g.1_4 ~~ sat.g.1_4
sat.g.1_5 ~~ sat.g.1_5

sat.g.2_1 ~~ sat.g.2_1
sat.g.2_2 ~~ sat.g.2_2
sat.g.2_3 ~~ sat.g.2_3
sat.g.2_4 ~~ sat.g.2_4
sat.g.2_5 ~~ sat.g.2_5

#Residual Covariances
sat.g.1_1 ~~ sat.g.2_1
sat.g.1_2 ~~ sat.g.2_2
sat.g.1_3 ~~ sat.g.2_3
sat.g.1_4 ~~ sat.g.2_4
sat.g.1_5 ~~ sat.g.2_5
"

fac3.script <- "
#Measurement Model

#Loadings
efa("efa")*f1 +
efa("efa")*f2 +
efa("efa")*f3 =~ sat.g.1_1 + sat.g.1_2 + sat.g.1_3 + sat.g.1_4 + sat.g.1_5 + sat.g.2_1 + sat.g.2_2 + sat.g.2_3 + sat.g.2_4 + sat.g.2_5

#Residual Variances
sat.g.1_1 ~~ sat.g.1_1
sat.g.1_2 ~~ sat.g.1_2
sat.g.1_3 ~~ sat.g.1_3
sat.g.1_4 ~~ sat.g.1_4
sat.g.1_5 ~~ sat.g.1_5

sat.g.2_1 ~~ sat.g.2_1
sat.g.2_2 ~~ sat.g.2_2
sat.g.2_3 ~~ sat.g.2_3
sat.g.2_4 ~~ sat.g.2_4
sat.g.2_5 ~~ sat.g.2_5

#Residual Covariances
sat.g.1_1 ~~ sat.g.2_1
sat.g.1_2 ~~ sat.g.2_2
sat.g.1_3 ~~ sat.g.2_3
sat.g.1_4 ~~ sat.g.2_4
sat.g.1_5 ~~ sat.g.2_5
"

When I fit these...(Defaulting to geomin rotation, so factor correlations are estimated)

sat.defa1.fit <- cfa(fac1.script , data = commitmentQ)
sat.defa2.fit <- cfa(fac2.script , data = commitmentQ)
sat.defa3.fit <- cfa(fac3.script , data = commitmentQ)

And compare them...

anova(sat.defa1.fit, sat.defa2.fit, sat.defa3.fit)

I get 30 df for 1-factor, 21 for 2-factor, and 13 for 3-factor

This checks out for the 1-factor model. Following ye ol' p(p+1)/2 formula:

knowns: 10(10+1)/2 = 55

1-factor model is estimating 10 factor loadings, 10 residual variances, 5 residual covariances = 25 estimates

df for 1-factor: 55 - 25 = 30. So far, so good.

To move to a 2-factor, then, would involve estimation of 10 additional loadings (onto second factor) and a correlation between F1 and F2. So estimating 11 additional things (36)
df for 2-factor should be 55 - 36 = 19

But for this model, I get 21 (df diff of 9, instead of 11)

The problem seems to compound for the 3-factor model:

Should be estimating 48 elements (adding 20 new factor loadings vs. 1 factor model + 3 factor correlations), so df should be 7, while anova returns 13.

Any idea of what's going on here? I've looked at nrow() of each model (subtracting of fixed variances for identification/scale-setting) and it corresponds to my counts of # of ests for each model.

I've also disabled meanstructure estimation (not that is was estimating anyways) just in case, to no avail.
